Systems and Networking

AI chips are wired together 72 to a rack and run as one computer. Many firms can assemble the racks, but lasers for the optical links between them were scarce in 2026.

Systems and Networking, stage 14 of 15Next stage: 15 Data Centers and Power

ConcentrationExtremeHigh

In plain terms

One AI chip is not enough to train a model. So seventy-two of them are wired together in a rack, a cabinet the size of a wardrobe, and run as one computer. Each chip sits on its own board and draws more than a thousand amps, several times the current a whole house is wired to carry. The chips have to swap results with each other all the time. A copper wire can carry those signals only a few meters before they fade, so the longer links send them as light down glass fiber. Many companies can build the rack, but in 2026 the lasers that send the light were scarce.

In short

In March 2026 Nvidia agreed to invest $2 billion in the laser maker Lumentum, alongside a multibillion-dollar purchase commitment and rights to future capacity for advanced laser components[1]. Indium phosphide is used in high-speed lasers for optical communications, and China produced 70 percent of the world's indium in 2025[2].

On 4 February 2025 China added indium phosphide substrates, the wafers the lasers are grown on, to its export control list[3]. AXT, a US-listed maker of those wafers, does all its manufacturing in China[3]. In its filing for the quarter to June 2026, AXT said it could not estimate when it would resume shipping the wafers to the United States[3].

Why substitution is possible
UALink is an open specification for the same job as NVLink[12]. AMD's Helios rack, launched in July 2026, runs it over Ethernet[13]. Since May 2025 Nvidia's NVLink Fusion program has let other firms' custom chips use NVLink, so the dependence on Nvidia stays[14].
Where China stands

Chinese firms such as InnoLight assemble high-speed optical modules in volume, at sites including Suzhou and, since 2019, Thailand[10]. In February 2025 China put indium under new export restrictions[2]. The same month it began requiring export permits for indium phosphide substrates, the wafers the lasers are grown on[3].

Where the US stands

Coherent broke ground in Sherman, Texas, in June 2026 on an expansion of its indium phosphide factory[15]. In August 2026 Nvidia said that Wistron's new plant in Fort Worth, Texas, was producing its GB300 superchips and that Foxconn was building a factory in Houston[16].

See it in 3D in the interactive chapter

Before a chip package can compute, it has to be built into a machine. Building that machine is a separate industry from making the package.

How it works

An accelerator (the AI chip) ships as a module, the chip package on a small board with the circuits that feed it power. Nvidia calls its version SXM, and the open-standards equivalent is the Open Compute Project's accelerator module. Eight modules bolt onto a baseboard that carries their power and the links between them. On Nvidia's baseboard, switch chips pass data between any two modules at full speed.

Rack-scale systems drop the baseboard and put the chips on trays stacked in the rack. An Nvidia GB300 NVL72 holds 18 compute trays plus nine switch trays, 72 GPUs in all, and draws up to 142 kW[17]. The newer Vera Rubin NVL72 uses the same rack footprint[18]. SemiAnalysis estimated in August 2025 that a GB200 NVL72 rack cost a typical hyperscaler $3.1 million, or about $3.9 million with networking, storage and other items[6].

Inside the rack the trays reach each other over copper[17]. Between neighboring racks, the signal can travel up to 7 meters over active electrical cables, a type of copper cable sold by firms such as Credo[19]. Longer links run on glass fiber, with an optical transceiver at each end. A laser in the sending transceiver turns the electrical signal into pulses of light, and a detector in the receiving one turns the pulses back into current.

The accelerators in an AI cluster exchange data over two networks that are not interchangeable. Scale-up connects anywhere from a few dozen accelerators to thousands closely enough that they can read each other's memory. It runs at terabytes per second. Scale-out joins those groups to one another at hundreds of gigabits per second. A byte is eight bits, so each GPU in a GB300 NVL72 has nine times as much bandwidth for scale-up as for scale-out, SemiAnalysis calculated in January 2026[20].

A model too big for one accelerator is split across many. The parts that exchange data constantly stay inside the scale-up group, while whole blocks of layers can sit on different groups across the slower scale-out network[21]. So scale-up bandwidth limits how efficiently a large model trains.

Variants and trade-offs

Scale-up: NVLink, UALink and Google's torus

The designs differ in how many accelerators can share one pool of memory.

  • NVLink and NVSwitch. Nvidia's per-GPU bandwidth went from 900 GB/s in NVLink 4 to 1,800 in NVLink 5, and the rack's own network moves 130 TB/s on Blackwell[22]. Nvidia's Rubin launch release of January 2026 gives NVLink 6 as 3,600 GB/s per GPU and 260 TB/s for a Vera Rubin NVL72 rack[23]. As of October 2026, Nvidia's NVLink product page still lists preliminary figures of 3,000 GB/s and 216 TB/s[22].
  • UALink. The open specification runs 200 Gb/s per lane, four lanes to a station for 800 Gb/s, and can address up to 1,024 endpoints in one group[12]. AMD's Helios rack, launched in July 2026, joins 72 GPUs and runs UALink over Ethernet for its scale-up network[13].
  • Google's 3D torus. Google wires 64 of its Ironwood TPU accelerators into each rack, called a cube[24]. Inside the cube each chip links directly to six others, in a three-dimensional grid that Google calls a 3D torus[24]. Optical circuit switches join cubes into superpods of 9,216 chips that can bypass a failed cube or link[24].

Scale-out: InfiniBand versus Ethernet

InfiniBand, a specialized network long used in supercomputers, was the main scale-out network when AI clusters were small and uniform, but Ethernet switch capacity grew quickly. Broadcom's Tomahawk 4 switched 25.6 Tbps on one chip in December 2019[25]. Tomahawk 5 reached 51.2 Tbps in August 2022, and Broadcom said it had doubled the bandwidth about every two years since 2014[26]. Tomahawk 6 doubled it again to 102.4 Tbps in June 2025[27]. In June 2025 the Ultra Ethernet Consortium published its 1.0 specification, a set of Ethernet-based communication protocols for AI and supercomputing that covers transport, congestion control and direct memory access[28].

Nvidia sells switches and network cards for both InfiniBand and Ethernet. Its data center revenue reached $89.0 billion in the quarter to July 2026, up 117 percent from a year earlier[29]. In the quarter before, it credited its data center growth to Blackwell 300 products and to demand for its "InfiniBand, Spectrum-X Ethernet, and NVLink" solutions[7].

Optics: pluggable, then co-packaged

A cluster needs several transceivers, the modules that turn electricity into light and back, for each accelerator. Their power cost is one reason Broadcom and Nvidia are moving the optics out of pluggable modules and into the switch chip's own package, a design called co-packaged optics. Broadcom's Tomahawk 6 Davisson cuts optical interconnect power by 70 percent compared with traditional pluggable modules[30]. It keeps its lasers in field-replaceable modules[30]. Nvidia's Spectrum-X Photonics switches, announced in March 2025, reach 512 ports of 800 gigabits and use four times fewer lasers than traditional designs[31]. Nvidia builds them on its Spectrum-6 switch design[23]. In August 2026 Nvidia said its Spectrum-6 switch systems, with pluggable or co-packaged optics, were arriving at AI data centers around the world[32].

Who makes it

Chinese makers of optical modules have built plants outside China. InnoLight has run a plant in Thailand since 2019, alongside its sites in Suzhou and Taiwan[10]. The Thai subsidiary of Eoptolink, another Chinese module maker, lists sites in Chonburi and Rayong[33].

The Federal Communications Commission publishes a Covered List of equipment and services judged to pose an unacceptable risk to US national security or to the security and safety of US persons[34]. Its July 2026 order bars new authorizations for devices that contain logic-bearing hardware components produced by firms on that list[35]. Commenters in the record named optical transceivers as one such component[36]. As of 16 October 2026, the Covered List did not include InnoLight or Coherent[37].

AI data centers were straining supplies of the lasers inside those modules and pushing up their prices, Nikkei Asia reported in May 2026[5]. Nvidia had agreed in March 2026 to invest $2 billion in one laser maker, Lumentum, alongside a multibillion-dollar purchase commitment and future capacity access rights for advanced laser components[1]. Coherent, another laser maker, broke ground in Sherman, Texas, in June 2026 on an expansion of its indium phosphide factory[15].

Indium phosphide is used in the high-speed laser diodes and photodetectors for optical communications[2]. China accounted for 70 percent of world indium production in 2025[2]. In February 2025 China's Ministry of Commerce placed indium under new export restrictions[2].

Broadcom's AI chips include custom accelerators and Ethernet switch chips[38]. In its annual report for fiscal 2025, Broadcom said that distributors and equipment makers account for most of its chip sales, and that it builds custom accelerators to each customer's specifications[38]. Its AI semiconductor revenue reached $16.7 billion in the third quarter of fiscal 2026, up 221 percent from a year earlier[8]. Marvell, another US firm, also builds custom AI chips to each customer's specifications and sells Ethernet switch chips, its annual report for fiscal 2026 says[39]. Marvell's five-year agreement with Amazon Web Services, announced in December 2024, covers custom AI chips alongside the optical and networking parts that go with them[40].

Taiwanese firms do much of the physical assembly. Foxconn booked NT$8.1 trillion of revenue in 2025, up 18 percent, and cloud and networking was its largest product category in the fourth quarter[9]. In the same results release, its chairman called Foxconn the world's largest AI server provider[9].

Some assembly is moving to the United States. In April 2025 Nvidia said it was building supercomputer manufacturing plants in Texas, with Foxconn in Houston and Wistron in Dallas[41]. It expected mass production to ramp up in the following 12 to 15 months[41]. In August 2026 Nvidia said Wistron's new plant in Fort Worth, Texas, near Dallas, was producing its GB300 superchips and Foxconn was building its factory in Houston[16].

The chokepoint

In October 2025 Nvidia said more than 50 makers of systems and components were gearing up for the Vera Rubin NVL72, whose design follows its MGX rack architecture[18]. In its filing for the quarter to July 2026, Nvidia said the complexity of producing its data center systems had caused production delays[29].

Four components that go into the rack take longer to replace.

  • Indium phosphide laser capacity. In March 2026 Nvidia agreed to invest $2 billion in Coherent, alongside a multibillion-dollar purchase commitment and future access and capacity rights for Coherent's advanced laser and optical networking products[11].
  • Indium phosphide substrates. China added indium phosphide substrates, the wafers the lasers are grown on, to its export control list on 4 February 2025[3]. AXT, a US-listed maker of these wafers, does all its manufacturing in China[3]. In its filing for the quarter to June 2026, AXT called the export permits the most significant challenge it faces[3]. It said it could not estimate when it would resume shipping the wafers to the United States[3]. The same filing names Sumitomo and JX as AXT's competitors in indium phosphide[3].
  • NVSwitch. Nvidia's annual report for fiscal 2026 lists NVLink interconnects and switches among its own networking products[4]. UALink is an open standard designed for accelerator communications within one scale-up group[12]. Since May 2025 Nvidia's NVLink Fusion program has let other firms' custom chips use NVLink, including CPUs that Fujitsu and Qualcomm plan to connect to Nvidia GPUs[14].
  • High-layer-count circuit boards. TTM Technologies, an American circuit board maker, says its circuit board competitors are mostly based in China and Taiwan[42]. Nitto Boseki, a Japanese glass fiber maker, makes NE-glass, a glass cloth that absorbs less signal, for the boards in data center switches and routers[43]. See Substrates and PCBs.

Optical module assembly can move, as InnoLight's high-volume plant in Thailand, opened in 2019, shows[10].

Review questions

Open a question to see its answer.

What is an AI rack?

A cabinet of 72 AI chips wired together to run as one computer.

The chips swap results with each other constantly. Reread: How it works

Why do the longer links between AI chips carry signals as light?

Copper carries the signals only a few meters.

Active copper cables carry the signal up to 7 meters between racks. Beyond that a laser turns the signal into pulses of light that travel down glass fiber. Reread: How it works

Which parts of an AI rack are hardest to replace?

Nvidia's NVLink switch chips, which connect the AI chips in a rack, and the lasers for the optical links.

By contrast, more than 50 makers of systems and components were gearing up for Nvidia's Vera Rubin NVL72 rack in October 2025, Nvidia said. Reread: The chokepoint

What does China control in the optical links?

About 70 percent of the world's 2025 output of indium, the raw material for the lasers.

Since February 2025 China has required export permits for indium phosphide substrates, the wafers the lasers are grown on. Chinese firms also assemble high-speed optical modules in volume. Reread: The chokepoint
